blocks.text: Most useful work is not a single action, it is a small sequence of actions that build on each other. Search for something, summarize what you found, then send that summary somewhere.

No single tool does all three of those jobs. Tool composition is the practice of chaining separate tools together so the output of one becomes the input of the next, producing a result none of them could produce alone.

This lesson looks at how that chaining actually happens, who decides the order of steps, what happens when a step in the middle fails, and how to choose between composing tools on the client versus building one composite tool on the server.
1. What Tool Composition Actually Means
Tool composition means combining two or more individual tool calls into a sequence that accomplishes a goal none of the tools reach by themselves.
Each tool still does one narrow job. The value comes from the order and the way data flows from one call into the next.
This is different from a tool simply having many parameters. Composition is about chaining separate calls, not adding more options to one call.

blocks.title: Composition is about sequence, not size
blocks.content: A single tool with a huge parameter list is still one tool. Composition specifically means multiple distinct tool calls, run in some order, feeding each other.

blocks.text: 2. A Simple Example: Search, Then Summarize, Then Send

blocks.alt: A Simple Example: Search, Then Summarize, Then Send
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163044-983157628.png
Picture three tools that already exist on their own. A search tool that returns raw web results. A summarize tool that condenses text. A send tool that delivers a message.
None of them can email someone a summary of today's news by itself. Chained together, in the right order, they can.

items: search tool: takes a query, returns a list of raw results
summarize tool: takes text, returns a shorter version
send tool: takes a recipient and a message, delivers it

blocks.text: The output of search feeds summarize, and the output of summarize feeds send. That handoff is the entire idea of composition.
3. Why No Single Tool Can Do This Alone
It would be possible to build one giant tool that searches, summarizes, and sends internally. Many teams do exactly that, and we will get to when it makes sense later in this lesson.
But most tools are kept small and focused on purpose. A search tool is useful on its own for a hundred other tasks that have nothing to do with summarizing or sending.
Keeping tools narrow means they can be recombined in new ways later, which is exactly what composition takes advantage of.
4. Two Models: Client Side Orchestration vs a Server Side Composite Tool

blocks.alt: Two Models: Client Side Orchestration vs a Server Side Composite Tool
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163045-664683381.png
There are two fundamentally different ways to get a chain like search, summarize, send to happen.
In the first, the LLM itself decides the order, calling each small tool one at a time and reasoning about the result before deciding the next step.
In the second, the server exposes one composite tool, and that tool internally calls search, summarize, and send itself, returning only the final result to the LLM.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model","Who decides the sequence","What the LLM sees"],"rows":[["Client side orchestration","The LLM, call by call","Every intermediate result"],["Server side composite tool","Fixed logic inside the server","Only the final output"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How an LLM Orchestrates a Chain Step by Step
When the client orchestrates, the LLM is given all three tools separately and reasons through the task turn by turn.
It calls search first, reads the raw results in its own context, decides they look usable, then calls summarize on them.
It reads the summary, decides it is short enough to send, then calls send with that summary as the message body.
Every loop iteration is one tool call, and the LLM alone is deciding when to stop calling tools and give a final answer.
6. Building a Composite Tool on the Server
The alternative is to fold the whole chain into a single tool the server exposes, often named something like research_and_notify.
From the LLM's point of view, this looks like one ordinary tool call with one set of arguments and one result.
Internally, the server code calls search, then summarize, then send, in a fixed order it controls, not the LLM.
The LLM never sees the raw search results or the intermediate summary text unless the server chooses to include them in the response.
7. Passing Data Between Steps
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163045-46949311.png
Whichever model you use, every step in a chain needs a clear contract for what it returns and what the next step expects as input.
A mismatch here, summarize expecting a plain string but search returning a list of objects, is one of the most common composition bugs.

items: Define a small, stable shape for each tool's output.
Convert between shapes explicitly rather than assuming they already match.
Keep transformation logic close to the step that produces the mismatched data.

blocks.title: Treat tool outputs like a real interface
blocks.content: Even informal tools benefit from a documented output shape. It saves the next step, and the next engineer, from guessing.

blocks.text: 8. Error Handling When a Step Fails Partway Through

blocks.alt: Error Handling When a Step Fails Partway Through
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163045-167449421.png
A chain of three steps has three separate places where something can go wrong, and each failure needs its own answer.
If search fails, there is nothing to summarize, so the whole chain should stop cleanly and say so.
If summarize fails after a successful search, the raw results still exist and might be worth returning instead of nothing at all.
If send fails after a successful search and summarize, the hardest case, the work is done but the last step did not land.
Notice the response shape changes depending on where the chain stopped, so whoever reads the result, an LLM or a person, knows exactly how far things got.
9. Partial Failure and Compensating Actions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163046-185990219.png
Some chains involve steps with side effects that are hard to undo, like send, which cannot be quietly cancelled once it succeeds.
When a later step fails after an earlier side effecting step succeeded, you generally cannot roll back, you can only report clearly what actually happened.
For chains where rollback matters, like reserving a seat then charging a card, a compensating action, an explicit undo step, needs to be part of the design from the start.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure point","What already happened","Reasonable response"],"rows":[["Search fails","Nothing","Fail fast, no partial state"],["Summarize fails","Search succeeded","Return raw results as a fallback"],["Send fails","Search and summarize succeeded","Report partial success, let the caller retry send only"]]}

blocks.text: 10. Retries Within a Composed Chain
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163047-306546008.png
Not every failure deserves a full stop. A search tool timing out once is often worth a single retry before giving up.
Retries belong at the level of the step that failed, not the whole chain, so a flaky search does not force summarize and send to run twice.
A small, bounded retry count matters here. An unbounded retry loop on a broken step just delays an honest failure.
11. When It Makes Sense to Compose at the Client Level
Client side composition, letting the LLM call each small tool itself, is the right default when flexibility matters more than a fixed sequence.
It shines when the exact steps needed cannot be predicted ahead of time, one request might need search and summarize, another might need search, translate, and send.

items: The order of steps genuinely varies request to request.
You want the LLM to inspect intermediate results and change course.
The individual tools are already useful on their own, outside this one chain.
You are still exploring what chains are actually useful, before locking anything in.

blocks.text: 12. When It Makes Sense to Build a Single Composite Server Tool
A server side composite tool is the better choice when the same sequence runs the same way, every single time, with no real branching.
It also wins when intermediate data is large, sensitive, or simply not useful for the LLM to see, like a full raw search dump before summarizing.

items: The sequence never changes, search then summarize then send, always in that order.
Intermediate results are noisy, large, or contain data that should not sit in the LLM's context.
You want to guarantee the steps run atomically as one unit, with one clear error contract.
Fewer round trips to the LLM meaningfully reduces cost or latency for a high volume task.

blocks.title: Composite tools trade flexibility for reliability
blocks.content: Folding a chain into one tool makes it faster and more predictable, but it also fixes the sequence in place. Changing the chain later means changing server code, not just a prompt.

blocks.text: 13. A Decision Table for Choosing Between the Two
Most real decisions come down to a small handful of questions about the task at hand.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question","Leans client side composition","Leans server side composite tool"],"rows":[["Does the sequence ever change?","Yes, often","No, always the same"],["Should the LLM see intermediate results?","Yes, useful context","No, just noise"],["How sensitive is latency or cost?","Not critical","Very important"],["Are the small tools useful on their own?","Yes","Not really, only used together"]]}

blocks.text: 14. Observability Across a Composed Chain
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163047-788460810.png
Whichever model you pick, you eventually need to answer a simple question: where exactly did this chain get to before something went wrong.
Logging each step with its own status, timing, and error, if any, turns a chain from a black box into something you can actually debug.
This is just as valuable inside a composite server tool as it is across separate client orchestrated calls, the LLM does not need to see these logs for them to be useful to you.
Worked Example: A Daily Digest Chain
Imagine a task: search for news on a topic, summarize the top results, then send the summary by email every morning.
Because the sequence never varies and the raw search text is not something anyone needs to read, this is a strong candidate for a server side composite tool.
One tool call from the LLM's side, three real steps underneath, and a clear result no matter where the chain stops.
Common Mistakes

items: Letting one failed step silently swallow the whole chain with no indication of how far it got.
Building a giant composite tool for a sequence that actually needs to vary request to request.
Exposing every raw intermediate result to the LLM when most of it is unnecessary noise.
Retrying an entire chain from the start instead of retrying only the step that failed.
Assuming a side effecting step like send can always be undone if a later step fails.
Skipping logging on individual steps, leaving no way to tell where a composite tool actually broke.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the search, summarize, send example from this lesson and implement it two ways.

items: First, as three separate tools the LLM calls one at a time, watching how it decides the order itself.
Second, as one composite research_and_notify tool with the error handling shown in this lesson.
Then force a failure in the summarize step on purpose and compare how each version reports what happened.

blocks.text: Notice how much more control you have over the exact error message in the composite version, versus how much more flexible the client orchestrated version feels when you change the task slightly.
Key Takeaway
Tool composition is what turns a handful of narrow tools into real capability, chaining search, summarize, and send into something none of them do alone.

Choose client side orchestration when flexibility matters, choose a server side composite tool when the sequence is fixed and reliability matters more, and always plan for the step that fails partway through.
